title: Analytical & Instrumental Techniques
tagline: Turn a clear tube of liquid into numbers you can defend: how the instruments of a biochemistry lab actually work.
overview: A foundation module on the measurements that underpin biochemistry and molecular biology. It begins with the habits of good measurement (accuracy, precision, error, solution and buffer preparation, calibration) and then works through the main families of technique: UV-visible spectrophotometry and protein and nucleic acid assays, fluorescence, infrared and circular dichroism, centrifugation, chromatography, electrophoresis, mass spectrometry and NMR, and immunoassays with labelled detection. Each unit is organised as a skills-and-technique module: what the instrument measures, the principle, how to prepare a sample, how to calibrate, how to read the result and what usually goes wrong. The topics are the standard content of a Level 2 analytical and instrumental techniques course for biochemistry students.
whyItMatters: Every claim in biochemistry rests on a measurement: an enzyme rate, a protein concentration, a band on a gel, a peak in a chromatogram, a mass. If you understand how the instrument produces the number, you can tell when to trust it and when something has gone wrong, and that judgement is the difference between a technician and a scientist.
careerLinks: Analytical and quality control laboratories in pharmaceutical, food and beverage industries
Research assistant or laboratory scientist in biochemistry, proteomics and molecular biology
Instrument application specialist or technical sales in life-science companies
studyTips: For each technique write a one-line answer to four questions: what is measured, what is the principle, what is the calibration, what are the interferences. Revise from these cards.
Do the arithmetic yourself first (dilutions, Beer-Lambert, Rf, molecular weight from a gel) and only then check against a tool. Calculation errors are the commonest practical mistakes.
Sketch a block diagram of every instrument (source, sample, selector, detector, readout). Many different instruments follow this same pattern.
In every practical, record units, blanks and replicates. If a result looks odd, the notes you kept will be the way you find out why.
Always ask: what would a failed experiment look like in this technique? Knowing the failure pattern teaches the principle.

units.title: Measurement, Error, Solutions and Buffers
units.hook: Two students run the same assay with the same enzyme and get answers that differ by thirty percent. Neither made an obvious mistake; one pipetted a viscous solution quickly, the other made a buffer at the wrong temperature. Good analysis begins with the unglamorous craft of measuring and mixing properly.
learningObjectives: Distinguish accuracy from precision and random from systematic error, and give examples from a biochemistry lab
Report results with sensible significant figures, units and an estimate of uncertainty (mean, standard deviation, replicates)
Prepare solutions of a stated molarity, percent and dilution using C1V1 = C2V2
Choose and prepare a buffer for a target pH using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
Calibrate a pH meter and use it correctly, including the effect of temperature
Use micropipettes correctly and check their performance

keyConcepts.definition: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated measurements to each other. A miscalibrated balance can give very precise but inaccurate results.

Random errors scatter results about the mean and are reduced by replicates; systematic errors push all results the same way (a zero error, a wrong standard) and are found only by calibration and controls.
The standard deviation describes the spread of repeated measurements. Technical replicates test the measurement; biological replicates test the variability of the system.
The digits that carry information. Report a result no more precisely than the least precise measurement that went into it.
Molarity is moles per litre. When diluting, moles are conserved so C1V1 = C2V2; a dilution factor is the final volume divided by the aliquot volume.
pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]). A buffer is most effective within about one pH unit of its pKa, where both forms are present in comparable amounts.

Choose a buffer whose pKa is near the desired pH and that does not interfere with the assay (phosphate inhibits some enzymes and precipitates calcium; Tris is amine-reactive and its pH shifts with temperature).
The pKa of some buffers changes with temperature; Tris falls by roughly 0.03 pH units for each degree of warming, so adjust the pH at the temperature of use.
A calibration relates instrument response to known standards. A blank contains everything except the analyte, and is used to subtract background.

deeper.beginner: Measuring is like cooking from a recipe: if the cup is the wrong size every dish will be consistently wrong (systematic error), and if you eyeball the amount each time the results will wobble (random error). A buffer is a chemical shock absorber that keeps pH steady when small amounts of acid or base enter; it works best near its pKa. Where the analogy breaks: a shock absorber has a fixed capacity, and so does a buffer, so a buffer at too low a concentration will fail when the reaction produces enough acid.
deeper.intermediate: Hands-on skills: (1) Check a micropipette by dispensing water onto a balance (1 mL of water weighs about 1 g at room temperature) and calculate mean and coefficient of variation of ten dispenses. Practise reverse pipetting for viscous liquids such as glycerol. (2) Prepare 100 mL of 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5 starting from solid Tris base and HCl: weigh Tris, dissolve in most of the volume, adjust pH with HCl at the temperature of use, make up to volume. (3) Prepare a 10x stock and dilute to 1x, calculating volumes with C1V1 = C2V2. (4) Calibrate a pH meter with two or three standard buffers that bracket the target pH, rinse the electrode between buffers, and check the slope. (5) Calculate the ratio of base to acid forms needed for a pH 7.0 phosphate buffer (pKa2 is about 7.2). Always label the date, composition and storage conditions on every solution you make.
deeper.advanced: Real buffer behaviour deviates from the ideal because pKa depends on ionic strength and temperature and because activity, not concentration, determines pH; this is why you should adjust pH after adding salts and avoid diluting a concentrated stock without re-checking. Buffer capacity is greatest at pH = pKa and scales with total buffer concentration. Some buffers interact with the system: borate binds cis-diols, phosphate and citrate chelate divalent metal ions, Good's buffers such as HEPES can form radicals under light and interfere with some assays. Uncertainty analysis combines contributions from pipetting, weighing and readings; for a calculated result you propagate errors (relative errors add in quadrature for products and quotients). Method validation uses terms such as limit of detection, limit of quantification, linearity, recovery and repeatability, and these appear in regulated laboratories.

commonMistakes: Quoting results with more decimal places than the measurement can support.
Adjusting the pH of a buffer at one temperature and using it at another, especially with Tris.
Calibrating a pH meter with a single standard or with expired buffers.
Using a pipette outside its stated range or with a poorly seated tip and then trusting the volume.

selfCheck.question: A balance consistently reads 0.5 g too high. Repeated weighings of a standard give very similar values. This is best described as:
selfCheck.explanation: Results cluster tightly (precise) but away from the true value (inaccurate) because of a systematic offset that calibration would reveal.

selfCheck.question: You need 200 mL of 10 mM NaCl from a 1 M stock. What volume of stock do you take?
selfCheck.explanation: C1V1 = C2V2 gives V1 = (10 mM x 200 mL) / 1000 mM = 2 mL, which is then made up to 200 mL with water.

selfCheck.question: Which buffer is the best choice for holding pH 5.0?
selfCheck.explanation: A buffer works best within about one pH unit of its pKa, and acetate's pKa is closest to pH 5.0.

units.title: UV-Visible Spectrophotometry, Beer-Lambert and Quantitative Assays
units.hook: Shine a beam of light through a cuvette and the proportion that survives tells you how much of something is there. This one idea underlies protein assays, DNA quantification, most enzyme assays and a large share of clinical chemistry.
learningObjectives: Explain the components of a spectrophotometer (source, monochromator, cuvette, detector) and what each does
State and apply the Beer-Lambert law, A = epsilon c l, and convert between absorbance and transmittance
Record an absorbance spectrum, choose lambda max and prepare a blank correctly
Quantify nucleic acids and proteins from A260 and A280 and interpret purity ratios
Build a calibration (standard) curve, fit a line and calculate unknown concentrations with uncertainty
Run and interpret the Bradford and BCA protein assays and recognise their interferences

keyConcepts.definition: Transmittance T = I/I0; absorbance A = log10(I0/I) = -log10(T). Absorbance is dimensionless and is additive for several absorbing species at one wavelength.

A = epsilon x c x l, where epsilon is the molar absorptivity (M^-1 cm^-1), c the concentration and l the path length (usually 1 cm). It holds when the light is monochromatic and the solution is dilute and non-interacting.

A property of a molecule at a given wavelength and solvent. For NADH at 340 nm it is 6220 M^-1 cm^-1, which allows direct calculation of NADH concentration and is the basis of many dehydrogenase assays.
A cuvette containing everything except the analyte, used to set zero absorbance and remove contributions from buffer, reagents and cuvette.

An A260 of 1.0 corresponds roughly to 50 micrograms per millilitre of double-stranded DNA and about 40 micrograms per millilitre of RNA. A260/A280 near 1.8 suggests pure DNA and near 2.0 pure RNA; lower values suggest protein or phenol contamination.

Tryptophan and tyrosine absorb near 280 nm, so concentration can be estimated if the extinction coefficient is known (computable from sequence); it is quick but fails if nucleic acid or other absorbers are present.
A plot of response against known concentrations. Unknowns must fall within the range of the standards, which is also within the linear range of the instrument.

Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 binds proteins (especially basic and aromatic residues) and shifts its absorbance maximum from about 465 nm to 595 nm; sensitive but affected by detergents and varies between proteins.

Proteins reduce Cu2+ to Cu+ under alkaline conditions, and bicinchoninic acid then complexes Cu+ to give a purple product near 562 nm; tolerant of detergents but sensitive to reducing agents and copper chelators.

deeper.beginner: Think of a coloured drink: the darker it is, the less light gets through. Doubling the concentration doubles the absorbance, so a straight-line graph lets you read an unknown concentration from a drink of known strengths. The 'blank' is the clear water you use to tell the machine what zero looks like. Where the analogy breaks: the proportionality holds only in a limited range; very dark samples bend the line, so you must dilute them.
deeper.intermediate: Hands-on skills: (1) Record an absorbance spectrum (for example of potassium dichromate or a coloured dye) and identify lambda max. (2) Quantify a plasmid or genomic DNA sample by diluting 1 in 50 in buffer, reading A260 and A280, and calculating concentration (A260 x dilution factor x 50 ng per microlitre) and purity ratio. (3) Prepare a BSA standard series (for example 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mg/mL) and run a Bradford assay in triplicate; plot A595 against concentration, fit a line through the linear region (or a quadratic if the curve bends), and calculate the concentration of an unknown protein, accounting for its dilution. (4) Measure NADH-dependent activity by following A340 over time and convert the slope to micromoles per minute using epsilon. Always check that sample absorbance falls within the standards, that the blank is correct and that cuvettes are matched and clean (use quartz below about 340 nm).
deeper.advanced: Deviations from Beer-Lambert arise from stray light, polychromatic illumination (the finite bandwidth of the monochromator), chemical equilibria that change with concentration, fluorescence, scattering and refractive-index effects; absorbance measurements above about 1.5 to 2 are unreliable on many instruments. Scattering by turbid samples adds an apparent absorbance that is wavelength dependent, and is corrected by measuring at a wavelength where the analyte does not absorb. Microvolume spectrophotometers use very short path lengths and require careful handling. Protein assays differ in chemistry and bias: Bradford depends on the amino-acid composition (arginine, lysine, aromatic residues), BCA on the peptide backbone, cysteine, tyrosine and tryptophan; therefore a BSA standard may over- or underestimate a different protein, and the assay should be matched to the buffer. Calibration curves should be fitted with appropriate weighting and checked for residual structure; report the confidence interval of the predicted concentration, not just the best-fit value.

commonMistakes: Reading samples with absorbance far above the highest standard and extrapolating the line.
Using the wrong cuvette (plastic below 340 nm for UV measurements) or fingerprinted or scratched cuvettes.
Blanking with water when the sample is in buffer or contains reagent colour.
Using A280 or A260 on a sample that contains both protein and nucleic acid, then trusting the number.

A DNA sample diluted 1 in 20 has A260 of 0.50. About what is the DNA concentration in the undiluted sample?
selfCheck.explanation: 0.50 x 50 micrograms per mL x 20 = 500 micrograms per mL, using A260 of 1 as about 50 micrograms per mL for double-stranded DNA.

options: BCA is unaffected by reducing agents

units.title: Fluorescence, Infrared and Circular Dichroism Spectroscopy
units.hook: Absorbance tells you that a molecule soaked up light. Fluorescence asks what it did next. Infrared asks how its bonds vibrate, and circular dichroism asks how its shape twists the light. Together they let you watch a protein fold without ever touching it.
learningObjectives: Explain fluorescence using the energy-level (Jablonski) picture, including Stokes shift and quantum yield
Distinguish excitation and emission spectra and choose suitable wavelengths and filters
Describe how intrinsic tryptophan fluorescence, quenching and FRET are used to study proteins
Explain the basis of infrared (including FTIR) spectroscopy and identify characteristic absorptions
Describe circular dichroism and interpret far-UV spectra for secondary structure
Compare absorption, fluorescence, IR and CD in terms of sensitivity, information and sample requirements

keyConcepts.definition: Emission of a photon when an excited molecule relaxes from its lowest excited singlet state to the ground state, typically within nanoseconds, at a longer wavelength than the light it absorbed.
The difference between the maxima of the excitation and emission spectra; it lets emission be separated from the exciting light by filters.
The fraction of absorbed photons that are re-emitted as fluorescence; it depends strongly on the environment of the fluorophore.
Tryptophan, excited near 280 nm, emits near 330 to 350 nm; emission shifts to longer wavelength when the residue is exposed to water, so unfolding can be followed.
Decrease in fluorescence due to collisions or complex formation with another molecule; can be used to measure accessibility and binding.
Resonance energy transfer from an excited donor to a nearby acceptor, with efficiency falling steeply with distance (typically sensitive over 1 to 10 nanometres), so it works as a molecular ruler.
Absorption of infrared light excites vibrations of chemical bonds; the position is expressed in wavenumbers (cm^-1) and depends on the bond and its environment, giving functional-group fingerprints.
Fourier-transform IR is a fast form of IR measurement. The amide I band near 1650 cm^-1 of proteins is sensitive to secondary structure.

The difference in absorption of left and right circularly polarised light by chiral molecules. Far-UV CD (about 190 to 250 nm) reports secondary structure; alpha-helices give negative bands near 208 and 222 nm.

deeper.beginner: Fluorescence is like a glow-in-the-dark toy: it absorbs one colour of light and gives back another, slightly lower-energy, colour. That change in colour lets an instrument detect the glow against a dark background, which makes the method extremely sensitive. IR spectroscopy is like listening to the notes of bond vibrations, and CD is like checking how a molecule handles twisted light, which depends on its shape. Where the analogy breaks: a toy glows reliably; a fluorophore's brightness depends on pH, solvent, temperature and quenchers, so a change in signal may not mean a change in amount.
deeper.intermediate: Hands-on skills: (1) Record the emission spectrum of a fluorescent standard (for example a dilute fluorescein solution in basic buffer) and identify excitation and emission maxima; then measure a dilution series and notice where the signal stops being linear because of the inner-filter effect. (2) Follow protein unfolding by tryptophan fluorescence with increasing urea or guanidine concentration and plot the shift in emission maximum. (3) Look at a CD spectrum of a helical protein and a mostly beta-sheet protein and describe the differences; note that the buffer must be transparent in the far UV (low-chloride phosphate buffers are preferred over Tris and chloride-rich buffers). (4) Using an FTIR spectrum of a simple compound, identify O-H, C=O and N-H stretches. Keep absorbance at the excitation wavelength below about 0.1 to avoid inner-filter effects, and always subtract the buffer spectrum.
deeper.advanced: Fluorescence lifetimes and anisotropy report on dynamics and binding (a large complex rotates slowly and keeps polarisation); time-resolved and single-molecule measurements reveal heterogeneity hidden in ensemble averages. FRET efficiency depends on the sixth power of distance, E = 1 / (1 + (r/R0)^6), with R0 the Forster distance for the pair, so small distance changes near R0 give large signal changes; orientation factors and photobleaching complicate quantitation. CD secondary-structure estimation uses deconvolution against reference spectra (for example CDSSTR, SELCON3 or BeStSel), and results depend on the quality of the concentration measurement and path length; near-UV CD reports on tertiary-structure asymmetry around aromatic residues. IR of aqueous protein samples is complicated by the strong absorption of water, usually overcome with D2O or attenuated total reflectance. For choosing a technique, consider that fluorescence has very high sensitivity but low structural information, CD gives global structure content in solution at modest concentration, and IR gives bond-level information with minimal sample prep.

commonMistakes: Using too concentrated a sample for fluorescence, so that absorption of excitation light (inner-filter effect) distorts the signal.
Reading a CD spectrum in a chloride-rich or Tris buffer that absorbs strongly below 200 nm.
Assuming a drop in fluorescence always means less protein; it can mean quenching, pH change or photobleaching.
Interpreting IR peak positions without considering the solvent and hydrogen bonding.

selfCheck.question: Why can fluorescence emission be detected even though it is weak?
options: It occurs at the same wavelength as excitation
Emission is at a longer wavelength than excitation, so it can be isolated with filters from the exciting light
selfCheck.explanation: The Stokes shift separates emission from excitation, and detection against a dark background gives high sensitivity.

selfCheck.question: A protein's far-UV CD spectrum shows strong negative bands near 208 and 222 nm. What does this indicate?
options: Presence of a heme group only
selfCheck.explanation: Double minima near 208 and 222 nm are the signature of alpha-helical content.

selfCheck.question: FRET efficiency changes strongly with:
options: The colour of the sample tube
The distance between donor and acceptor (inverse sixth power dependence)
The molecular mass of the protein only
The pH of the water bath
selfCheck.explanation: Energy transfer falls with the sixth power of donor-acceptor distance, making FRET a sensitive measure of nanometre-scale distances.

units.title: Centrifugation and Cell Fractionation
units.hook: Spin a tube fast enough and the contents sort themselves by size and density: nuclei, then mitochondria, then membrane fragments, then the soluble cytoplasm. Much of what we know about where biochemistry happens in the cell came from this simple trick.
learningObjectives: Calculate relative centrifugal force (RCF, in x g) from rotor radius and speed, and explain why g, not rpm, must be reported
Distinguish differential centrifugation, rate-zonal and isopycnic (equilibrium) density-gradient centrifugation
Describe how cells are homogenised and fractionated and how fractions are checked with marker enzymes
Select an appropriate rotor type and speed for pelleting cells, organelles or macromolecules
Apply safety rules, including rotor balancing, for centrifuge use
Explain how the Meselson-Stahl experiment used density-gradient centrifugation

keyConcepts.definition: RCF = 1.118 x 10^-5 x r x (rpm)^2 with r the radius in cm. The same rpm gives different forces in different rotors, so protocols specify x g.

A measure of how fast a particle sediments under a given force, in Svedberg units (10^-13 seconds). It depends on mass, shape and density, and is not additive (ribosome subunits 30S + 50S form a 70S particle).

Repeated spins at increasing force: low speed pellets nuclei and cell debris, medium speed pellets mitochondria and lysosomes, high speed pellets microsomes (ER fragments), and the supernatant is the cytosol.
Sample is layered on top of a pre-formed gradient (usually sucrose) and separated by sedimentation rate; the run is stopped before the particles reach the bottom.

Particles move through a gradient (for example caesium chloride or iodixanol) until they reach the position where their density equals that of the medium, so separation depends only on buoyant density.
Gentle disruption of cells in an isotonic, buffered, cold medium, so that organelles remain intact and enzymes remain active.

Enzymes characteristic of a compartment, used to assess purity and yield of a fraction (for example succinate dehydrogenase for mitochondria, catalase for peroxisomes, lactate dehydrogenase for cytosol).
Swing-bucket rotors give clean separations in gradients; fixed-angle rotors give shorter pelleting paths and are used for high-speed pelleting; vertical rotors shorten isopycnic runs.

deeper.beginner: Imagine swirling muddy water until the heavy sand drops and the lighter silt stays suspended. A centrifuge is a way of making gravity much stronger so that even tiny particles settle in minutes. Spinning at low speed pulls down the big, heavy things first; each faster spin collects smaller things. Where the analogy breaks: cell parts overlap in size and density, so each fraction is enriched rather than perfectly pure, which is why marker enzymes are used.
deeper.intermediate: Hands-on skills: (1) Convert a protocol written as 12,000 x g to rpm for your rotor using the manufacturer's radius, and vice versa. (2) Perform a differential centrifugation of liver or a plant tissue homogenate (or analyse provided data): spin at 600 to 1,000 x g to pellet nuclei, then 10,000 to 15,000 x g to pellet mitochondria, then about 100,000 x g to pellet microsomes. (3) Assay a marker enzyme in each fraction and calculate recovery (total activity in fractions divided by total in the homogenate) and enrichment (specific activity in the fraction divided by the starting specific activity). (4) Weigh and balance tubes to within the tolerance specified for the rotor; never run an unbalanced rotor. Keep samples at 4 degrees Celsius unless told otherwise, and check that tubes are rated for the speed and solvent used.
deeper.advanced: Sedimentation is described by the Svedberg equation, s = M(1 - v-bar rho) / (N f), where M is molar mass, v-bar the partial specific volume, rho the density of the medium, N Avogadro's number and f the frictional coefficient; analytical ultracentrifugation uses optical detection to measure sedimentation velocity and equilibrium directly in solution, giving mass, shape and binding information without matrix interactions. Density gradients can be self-forming (CsCl, iodixanol) or pre-formed (sucrose), each with its osmotic effects on organelles. Subcellular fractionation is increasingly combined with proteomics (for example LOPIT and related methods) to assign proteins to compartments, relying on statistical clustering because no fraction is pure. Safety and maintenance include rotor life limits, corrosion checks and use of aerosol-tight tubes when handling infectious material.

commonMistakes: Reporting a centrifugation in rpm without the rotor or radius, so it cannot be repeated.
Running with unbalanced tubes or tubes that are not rated for the speed, risking rotor failure.
Treating a pellet as pure; contaminants co-sediment and must be assessed with markers.
Homogenising too violently or in a hypotonic medium, which breaks organelles and releases enzymes.

selfCheck.question: Why should centrifugation protocols give speed in x g rather than rpm?
options: x g is a smaller number
The force depends on rotor radius as well as rpm, so rpm alone does not specify the same force in different rotors
x g is only used for DNA
selfCheck.explanation: RCF depends on both speed and radius; reporting x g makes the protocol reproducible with any rotor.

selfCheck.question: In differential centrifugation of a tissue homogenate, which fraction pellets first (at the lowest speed)?
selfCheck.explanation: The largest, densest structures such as nuclei and unbroken cells sediment at low force; smaller particles require progressively higher force.

selfCheck.question: Isopycnic centrifugation separates particles according to:
selfCheck.explanation: Particles move until the gradient density equals their own buoyant density, so shape and mass do not matter at equilibrium.

units.title: Chromatography: TLC, Column, Ion Exchange, Size Exclusion, Affinity and HPLC
units.hook: Pour a mixture onto a column and the components come out one after another, as if each had been given a different pace. That simple idea built protein purification, drug analysis, blood tests and much of modern biochemistry.
learningObjectives: Explain the basic principle of chromatography in terms of stationary phase, mobile phase and partitioning
Calculate Rf and retention time, and describe how resolution depends on efficiency, selectivity and retention
Perform and interpret thin-layer chromatography
Describe the mechanisms of ion exchange, size exclusion, affinity, hydrophobic interaction and reversed-phase chromatography
Design a simple multi-step purification of a protein and keep a purification table (yield, specific activity, fold purification)
Describe the components and operation of an HPLC system and interpret a chromatogram

keyConcepts.definition: In chromatography, the sample is carried by a mobile phase (liquid or gas) over a stationary phase. Components that interact more strongly with the stationary phase move more slowly.
In TLC, Rf = distance moved by the spot / distance moved by the solvent front (between 0 and 1). In column methods, retention time is the time between injection and the peak maximum.
How well two peaks are separated, combining peak spacing and peak width. A resolution of 1.5 or more is generally considered baseline separation.

Separates by net charge. A cation exchanger (negatively charged resin, for example carboxymethyl) binds positively charged proteins; elution uses increasing salt or a pH change. Whether a protein binds depends on pH relative to its pI.

Molecules are separated by size as they pass through porous beads; large molecules, which cannot enter the pores, elute first, followed by smaller ones. Used for polishing, desalting and estimating size.

Uses a specific interaction: for example His-tagged proteins bind nickel-NTA resin and are eluted with imidazole, GST-tagged proteins bind glutathione, and antibodies bind Protein A. Very high selectivity in one step.

Hydrophobic interaction chromatography uses high salt to promote binding to a mildly hydrophobic resin. Reversed-phase HPLC (for example a C18 column) uses a nonpolar stationary phase and a polar mobile phase with an organic gradient, widely used for peptides and small molecules.

High-performance liquid chromatography forces the mobile phase through a tightly packed column at high pressure with a pump, injector, column and detector (UV, fluorescence, or mass spectrometer), giving fast, reproducible, quantitative separations.

A record at each step of total protein, total activity, specific activity (activity per mg), yield (percent activity recovered) and purification fold (specific activity relative to the crude extract).

deeper.beginner: Chromatography is like a race through varied terrain: runners (molecules) who like the mud (stationary phase) run slowly, while those who prefer the open track (mobile phase) run fast. Over a long course they spread out and cross the finishing line one by one. In protein purification, you choose terrain that suits one feature: charge, size or a specific tag. Where the analogy breaks: molecules do not run at a steady pace but constantly jump between phases, which is what causes peaks to widen.
deeper.intermediate: Hands-on skills: (1) Run TLC of plant pigments or amino acids, mark the solvent front before drying, calculate Rf and visualise (ninhydrin for amino acids). (2) Pack or use a pre-packed gel-filtration column, apply a mixture of blue dextran (excluded volume), a coloured protein and a small dye, and collect fractions to determine elution volumes; use standards of known size to make a calibration curve of log molecular weight against elution volume. (3) Design an ion-exchange step: for a protein with pI 6.0 you could use an anion exchanger at pH 8 (the protein is negatively charged) and elute with a salt gradient. (4) Complete a purification table from provided data: from crude extract to a final affinity eluate, calculate specific activity, yield and fold. (5) Read an HPLC chromatogram, identify peaks by retention time against standards and quantify from peak area using a calibration curve. Equilibrate columns before use, degas and filter solvents and never let a column run dry.
deeper.advanced: Retention in liquid chromatography is described by the retention factor k = (tR - t0) / t0, selectivity alpha = k2/k1 and plate number N, which combine in the resolution equation Rs = (sqrt(N)/4) x ((alpha - 1)/alpha) x (k/(1 + k)); this tells you whether to improve efficiency (smaller particles, longer columns), selectivity (change phase or solvent) or retention. Gradient elution compresses peaks and shortens analyses of complex samples. In protein work, multi-step purification schemes use orthogonal principles (for example affinity, ion exchange, size exclusion) to remove different contaminants, and each step is balanced against yield and activity. Detection choices include UV absorbance, fluorescence, refractive index, conductivity and mass spectrometry; LC-MS combines separation with identification. Gas chromatography separates volatile compounds (or derivatives) and is common for fatty acids and metabolites. Analytical method validation covers specificity, linearity, accuracy, precision and robustness.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to mark the solvent front on a TLC plate before the solvent evaporates, so Rf cannot be calculated.
Overloading a column, which broadens peaks and ruins resolution; size-exclusion in particular needs small sample volumes.
Ignoring the pH relative to the protein's pI in ion exchange, so the protein binds the wrong way or not at all.
Reporting purification only as yield and not specific activity: a high yield of an impure protein is not a good purification.

units.title: Electrophoresis: Agarose, SDS-PAGE, Isoelectric Focusing and 2D Gels
units.hook: A tiny current, a slab of gel, and a mixture of molecules begins to march. In an hour you have a ladder of bands that tells you the size of a DNA fragment, the purity of a protein preparation, or whether your experiment worked at all.
learningObjectives: Explain how charge, size and shape determine the migration of molecules in an electric field and a gel matrix
Choose agarose or polyacrylamide and the appropriate gel percentage for a given DNA or protein size range
Run and interpret agarose gel electrophoresis of DNA, including the use of size markers and stains
Explain how SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size, including the roles of SDS, reducing agent and the stacking and resolving gels
Estimate molecular weight from a standard curve of log MW against relative mobility
Describe isoelectric focusing, 2D electrophoresis and native PAGE and when each is used

keyConcepts.definition: The velocity of a molecule per unit electric field, determined by its charge, size and shape and by the medium. In a gel, smaller molecules move faster than larger ones of the same charge density.

A polysaccharide gel with large pores, suited to DNA and RNA from about 100 base pairs to tens of kilobases. Lower percentages (0.7 percent) resolve large fragments; higher percentages (2 percent) resolve small ones.
DNA is uniformly negatively charged through its phosphate backbone, so it moves toward the positive electrode (anode) and its mobility is approximately proportional to the logarithm of its length.

A cross-linked synthetic gel with smaller, adjustable pores, used for proteins and for small DNA or RNA fragments needing single-base resolution. Acrylamide in solution is a neurotoxin, so wear gloves.

Sodium dodecyl sulfate binds proteins in a roughly constant ratio, denaturing them and giving a uniform negative charge per unit mass. With a reducing agent that breaks disulfide bonds, migration depends mainly on polypeptide size.
In the Laemmli system, a low-percentage, pH 6.8 stacking gel concentrates the sample into a sharp band before it enters the higher-percentage, pH 8.8 resolving gel where separation occurs.
A ladder of proteins or DNA fragments of known size run in the same gel. A plot of log MW against relative mobility (Rf) gives a calibration for estimating unknowns.
Proteins migrate in a pH gradient until they reach the pH equal to their pI, where their net charge is zero and they stop; this separates by pI.
IEF in the first dimension followed by SDS-PAGE in the second, spreading thousands of proteins in a plane by pI and size.

deeper.beginner: Think of a crowd walking through a forest with a steady wind pushing them forward: small people slip between the trees and travel far, large people get stuck and travel less. The gel is the forest, the electric field is the wind, and the bands are groups of people of the same size. SDS makes every protein carry the same charge per unit size so that only size matters. Where the analogy breaks: with unmodified (native) proteins, charge and shape also matter, so native gels do not give clean size information.
deeper.intermediate: Hands-on skills: (1) Agarose gel: prepare a 1 percent gel in TAE or TBE with a safe nucleic acid stain, load a DNA ladder and your samples with loading dye, run at a constant voltage (for example 5 to 8 V per cm of gel length) until the dye front has migrated far enough, and image. Estimate fragment sizes against the ladder. (2) Digest a plasmid with one or two restriction enzymes and predict the band pattern before running it. (3) SDS-PAGE: mix protein with sample buffer containing SDS and a reducing agent, heat, load alongside a protein ladder, run, and stain with Coomassie. Plot log MW against Rf for the standards, fit a straight line and calculate the size of an unknown band. (4) Troubleshoot: smiling bands (uneven heating), smeared lanes (overloading or degraded sample), no bands (wrong polarity, stain failure, little sample). Treat gel stains and acrylamide as hazardous and dispose of them properly.
deeper.advanced: In Laemmli discontinuous electrophoresis, chloride (leading ion) and glycine (trailing ion) create a moving boundary that stacks proteins in a thin zone because of the different mobilities at pH 6.8 and 8.8; proteins then unstack as glycine overtakes them in the resolving gel. SDS binding is on the order of 1.4 g per gram of protein, but glycoproteins, membrane proteins and highly basic or acidic proteins can run anomalously. Native PAGE and blue-native PAGE preserve complexes, and capillary electrophoresis offers high resolution and automation, as in modern DNA sequencers. For nucleic acids, pulsed-field gel electrophoresis separates megabase fragments by changing the field direction. Quantification of bands requires linear response of the stain (Coomassie, silver, fluorescent dyes have different dynamic ranges). 2D electrophoresis reveals post-translational modifications through shifts in pI, though it has been largely supplemented by mass-spectrometry-based proteomics for depth.

commonMistakes: Connecting the electrodes the wrong way round so that DNA runs off the gel into the buffer (DNA moves toward the positive electrode).
Overloading a lane, giving smeared, distorted bands that are impossible to size.
Forgetting the reducing agent or the heating step in SDS-PAGE sample preparation, giving extra bands from disulfide-linked complexes.
Using a single band position as a precise molecular weight; gel estimates are usually only accurate to about 10 percent.

It reaches the pH equal to its pI where its net charge is zero

units.title: Mass Spectrometry and NMR Spectroscopy
units.hook: Weigh a molecule so precisely that you can tell which amino acid it contains, or listen to the magnetic whisper of its atoms to map out its structure. These two tools are how modern biochemistry identifies and characterises molecules too small to see.
learningObjectives: Describe the three stages of a mass spectrometer (ionisation, mass analysis, detection) and the m/z concept
Distinguish ESI and MALDI ionisation and name common analysers (quadrupole, time-of-flight, ion trap, Orbitrap)
Explain tandem MS (MS/MS) and how peptide sequences are obtained, including the bottom-up proteomics workflow
Interpret simple mass spectra, including multiply charged ESI envelopes and isotope patterns
Explain the basic principle of NMR (nuclear spin, magnetic field, resonance, chemical shift) and interpret a simple 1H NMR spectrum
Compare MS and NMR in terms of sensitivity, information, sample requirements and typical applications

keyConcepts.definition: Mass-to-charge ratio, the quantity measured by a mass spectrometer. For an ion carrying z charges, m/z is the mass (in daltons) divided by z.
A soft ionisation method in which a liquid sample is sprayed through a charged needle, producing multiply charged ions of intact proteins and peptides; easily coupled to liquid chromatography.

Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionisation: the sample is co-crystallised with a light-absorbing matrix and a laser pulse generates mostly singly charged ions; often paired with a time-of-flight analyser.

Quadrupoles filter ions by m/z, time-of-flight (TOF) analysers time how long ions take to cross a flight tube, ion traps and Orbitraps store ions and measure their oscillation to give very high resolution and accuracy.

A selected ion is fragmented (for example by collision with gas) and the fragments are measured. For peptides, fragments produced at the peptide bonds give a ladder from which the sequence can be read or matched to a database.

Proteins are digested with a protease (usually trypsin, which cuts after lysine and arginine, except before proline), peptides are separated by LC and analysed by MS/MS, and spectra are matched to a protein sequence database.
Nuclei with spin (1H, 13C, 15N, 31P) in a strong magnetic field absorb radio-frequency radiation at frequencies that depend on their chemical environment.

The resonance position (in ppm, relative to a reference) that reflects the electronic environment of a nucleus; for example, protons next to electronegative atoms or in aromatic rings resonate at higher ppm.
In a 1H NMR spectrum, peak area is proportional to the number of equivalent protons, and spin-spin coupling splits peaks into patterns that reveal neighbouring protons (n neighbours give n+1 lines).

deeper.beginner: Mass spectrometry is a very precise set of scales for molecules: it turns them into charged particles, flings them through a field, and measures how they respond, giving their mass. NMR places molecules in a strong magnet and checks which radio frequencies their atomic nuclei respond to, which gives a fingerprint of the atoms' surroundings. Where the analogy breaks: mass spectrometers weigh ions in a vacuum, not molecules in water, so the sample must be ionised without destroying it, which took decades to develop for large biomolecules.
deeper.intermediate: Hands-on and interpretation skills: (1) Calculate m/z for a peptide at +1, +2 and +3 charge states, given its mass and the mass of a proton (1.007 Da). (2) Given a list of m/z values forming a multiply charged envelope, work out the charge of adjacent peaks and the molecular mass of the protein. (3) Walk through the bottom-up proteomics workflow on a gel band: in-gel digestion with trypsin, peptide extraction, LC-MS/MS, database search, and reporting protein identification with a false discovery rate. (4) Interpret a simple 1H NMR spectrum of ethanol or ethyl acetate, assigning peaks from chemical shift, integration and splitting. (5) Discuss which technique you would choose to confirm the identity of a purified recombinant protein (intact mass by ESI-MS plus peptide mapping) and which to determine the 3D structure of a small protein in solution (multi-dimensional NMR).
deeper.advanced: Mass accuracy in parts per million and resolving power determine whether you can distinguish molecules of similar mass; high-resolution instruments (Orbitrap, FT-ICR) can separate isotopic peaks and assign elemental composition. Quantitative proteomics uses isotope labelling (SILAC, TMT) or label-free methods, with data-dependent or data-independent acquisition, and requires statistical control of false discovery rate through target-decoy strategies. Post-translational modifications are located by their mass shifts in MS/MS spectra. In NMR, the signal arises from the small excess of spins aligned with the field (Boltzmann distribution) and is intrinsically insensitive, so higher fields and cryoprobes help; protein NMR uses isotope-labelled (15N, 13C) samples and multidimensional experiments such as HSQC, which gives one peak per backbone N-H pair and serves as a fingerprint of folding and ligand binding. Both techniques are core to metabolomics, structural biology and drug discovery, and increasingly complement cryo-EM and X-ray crystallography.

commonMistakes: Confusing m/z with mass: for multiply charged ions, the observed m/z is much smaller than the molecular mass.
Believing a database match is certain; protein identifications come with a score and a false discovery rate that must be reported.
Interpreting NMR peaks by chemical shift alone without integration and splitting.
Treating MS as automatically quantitative; ionisation efficiency varies between molecules and needs standards.

options: It cuts after lysine and arginine, producing peptides with a basic C-terminus that ionise and fragment well

units.title: Immunoassays, Western Blotting and Labelled Detection
units.hook: Antibodies are nature's molecular recognition tools, so specific that an assay built on them can detect a hormone at picomolar concentrations in a drop of blood. Add an enzyme, a fluorescent dye or a radioactive atom to the antibody, and the invisible becomes a measurable colour or click.
learningObjectives: Explain antibody-antigen binding and the roles of primary and secondary antibodies
Describe the formats and logic of direct, indirect, sandwich and competitive ELISA
Design the plate layout, controls and standard curve for a quantitative ELISA and analyse the data
Carry out and interpret a Western blot (transfer, blocking, antibody incubation, detection) including loading controls
Compare detection labels: enzymes (HRP, alkaline phosphatase), fluorophores and radioisotopes
Describe how radioisotopes are detected and the safety principles for handling them

keyConcepts.definition: Specificity is the ability to recognise one target among many; affinity is the strength of binding. Polyclonal antibodies recognise multiple epitopes; monoclonal antibodies recognise one epitope.
The primary antibody binds the target; a labelled secondary antibody binds the primary, amplifying signal and allowing one labelled reagent to detect many primaries.

Direct: labelled antibody detects antigen on the plate. Indirect: labelled secondary detects the primary. Sandwich: capture antibody, antigen, then detection antibody (most specific and sensitive). Competitive: signal falls as antigen in the sample increases.
Horseradish peroxidase (HRP) with TMB produces a blue product that turns yellow on acid and is read at 450 nm; alkaline phosphatase with p-nitrophenyl phosphate gives a yellow product read at 405 nm.
Blanks (no antigen), negative and positive controls, and omission of the primary antibody identify non-specific binding and confirm the assay works.

Proteins separated by SDS-PAGE are transferred to a nitrocellulose or PVDF membrane, blocked to prevent non-specific binding, probed with primary and enzyme-labelled secondary antibodies and detected by chemiluminescence or fluorescence.
A protein expected to be constant (for example actin, tubulin or GAPDH, or total protein stain) used to check that equal amounts were loaded when comparing samples.
Isotopes such as 3H, 14C, 32P, 35S and 125I allow extremely sensitive tracing of molecules, detected by liquid scintillation counting or autoradiography; use is restricted and regulated.
The time for half the radioactive atoms to decay (for example 14C about 5,730 years, 32P about 14.3 days, 35S about 87 days, 3H about 12.3 years); it affects planning, signal and waste handling.

deeper.beginner: An antibody is a lock-and-key molecule that recognises one specific shape. To make that recognition visible you attach something measurable to it: an enzyme that makes a coloured product, a fluorescent dye or a radioactive atom. In an ELISA, antibodies catch the target on a plastic plate and the colour that develops tells you how much is there. Where the analogy breaks: the lock is rarely perfect; an antibody may also bind other proteins weakly, which is why controls are so important.
deeper.intermediate: Hands-on skills: (1) Plan a sandwich ELISA on a 96-well plate: coat with capture antibody, block, add standards and samples in duplicate or triplicate, add detection antibody, add enzyme conjugate, wash thoroughly between steps, add substrate, stop the reaction and read absorbance at 450 nm. Include blanks and zero standards. (2) Plot absorbance against log concentration for standards, fit a four-parameter logistic curve (or a linear region), and calculate unknowns, ensuring samples fall within the curve and applying dilution factors. (3) Run a Western blot: after SDS-PAGE, transfer protein to a membrane, check transfer by reversible staining, block with milk or BSA, incubate with primary then secondary antibody, wash with buffer containing mild detergent, develop with chemiluminescent substrate and image. Normalise band intensities to a loading control. (4) Troubleshoot high background (insufficient blocking or washing, too much antibody), weak signal (inactive antibody, poor transfer) and non-specific bands (cross-reactivity, degradation). (5) Discuss safety, shielding, monitoring and waste for radioisotope experiments.
deeper.advanced: ELISA data are non-linear and best fitted with a four- or five-parameter logistic model; the working range, limit of detection and quantification, and the hook effect (falsely low signal at very high antigen in sandwich assays) must be considered. Assay validation includes spike-and-recovery, parallelism with dilution and cross-reactivity testing. Antibody validation is a major reproducibility issue: knockout or knock-down controls, orthogonal methods and recombinant antibodies give more confidence than catalogue descriptions. Western blot quantification requires signals within the linear range; chemiluminescence saturates easily, and fluorescent secondary antibodies or total-protein normalisation offer better linearity. Radiolabel experiments (for example pulse-chase, binding assays with 125I or 3H ligands) remain unmatched in sensitivity for some questions, but are being replaced where possible by non-radioactive alternatives. Immunoassays also form the basis of lateral-flow tests and clinical analysers.

commonMistakes: Using too little washing between ELISA steps, causing high background and poor reproducibility.
Interpreting a faint Western band as quantitative proof of protein level without a loading control or a linear detection range.
Running samples outside the standard curve and extrapolating, especially at the plateau where the curve is flat.
Assuming an antibody that works in one application (for example ELISA) will work in another (for example Western blot or immunofluorescence) without validation.
